summary.text: The Artemis program is NASA's effort to return humans to the Moon for the first time since Apollo and to build a permanent lunar base.
It was formally established in 2017, and as of 2026 it has flown two successful missions, Artemis I and Artemis II.
Each numbered mission launches an SLS rocket carrying an Orion spacecraft, and Artemis IV, targeted for 2028, is planned to be the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo.

items.prompt: Artemis II is described as broadly like Apollo 8. What set it apart?

options.label: It landed on the Moon surface itself
It skipped Moon orbit for a more distant flyby
It flew with no crew on board at all
It stayed in low Earth orbit the entire time

items.explain: Artemis II did not orbit the Moon and flew a more distant lunar flyby than the Apollo missions.

items.prompt: The third Artemis mission has a crew flying to Earth orbit, not the Moon. What will they do there?

options.label: Build the first pieces of a lunar base there
Fly past the Moon and splash down in the sea
Practise docking with commercial landers and test a suit
Send a lander down to the surface of the Moon

items.explain: The crew will conduct rendezvous and docking tests in Earth orbit with commercially developed lunar landers and test the AxEMU space suit.

items.prompt: What must happen before the crew of the first Artemis landing mission launches?

options.label: A separate crew must build a base on the surface
The SLS must be tested again with mannequins
Orion must fly alone to the Moon on its own rocket
A support flight must place a lander in lunar orbit

items.explain: Artemis IV depends on a prior support flight to place a lander in lunar orbit before SLS and Orion launch.

items.prompt: A newcomer asks why the Artemis rocket and capsule seem to use familiar parts. What explains it?

options.label: It reuses stages and engines recovered from the Saturn V
It reuses Shuttle-derived hardware, plus Orion from Constellation
It copies the design of a commercial rocket company
It is built from parts of an old Soviet moon rocket

items.explain: Artemis uses Space Shuttle-derived hardware such as the SLS core stage, RS-25 engines and boosters, along with Orion from the canceled Constellation program.

items.prompt: An earlier program, Constellation, was suspended after a review committee examined it. What did the committee conclude?

options.label: Its rockets had failed in testing
Its goals repeated what the Space Shuttle did
It was massively underfunded, and a 2020 Moon landing was impossible
It cost less than commercial options but took too long

items.explain: The Augustine Committee concluded that Constellation was massively underfunded and that a 2020 Moon landing was impossible, and the program was then suspended.

items.prompt: Artemis I flew with no crew and was a success overall. What problem did engineers find afterward?

options.label: Orion's heat shield wore away more than expected during reentry
Orion's parachutes failed to open at splashdown
The SLS engines shut down before the planned time
Orion missed the Moon and never reached lunar orbit

items.explain: Although the mission was successful overall, Orion's ablative heat shield experienced greater-than-expected erosion during reentry.

paragraphs.heading: What Artemis is
paragraphs.text: Artemis is a NASA-led program to send people back to the Moon for the first time since Apollo and to build a permanent base there. President Donald Trump formally set it up in 2017 through Space Policy Directive-1. By 2026 two missions had succeeded, Artemis I and Artemis II, and three more are planned by the close of 2028.

paragraphs.heading: The hardware
paragraphs.text: Each numbered mission is built around one launch of the Space Launch System, or SLS, a rocket carrying an Orion spacecraft. Much of SLS is borrowed from the Space Shuttle, including its core stage, RS-25 engines and solid rocket boosters. Orion, paired with the European Service Module, comes from the canceled Constellation program. The third core piece, the Human Landing System, is being developed by private companies under contract. Partnerships with other countries are governed by the Artemis Accords.

paragraphs.heading: Built on canceled plans
paragraphs.text: Artemis reuses parts of earlier NASA plans that were dropped. The Constellation program, set up by law in 2005 as the Space Shuttle neared retirement, was developing the Ares I and Ares V rockets along with Orion. In 2009 President Obama formed the Augustine Committee, which found Constellation badly underfunded and judged a 2020 Moon landing impossible, and Constellation was suspended. In April 2010 Obama canceled all of its parts except Orion.

paragraphs.heading: The first two flights
paragraphs.text: Orion's first launch on SLS, at first planned for 2016, slipped again and again before flying on November 16, 2022, as Artemis I, with mannequins and robotic payloads aboard. Orion spent about six days in a distant orbit around the Moon, then came home and landed in the Pacific under parachutes. The flight went well overall, though Orion's heat shield wore away more than expected on reentry. Artemis II, on April 1, 2026, was the first test with people aboard: four astronauts tested Orion in high Earth orbit, then looped around the Moon and returned. It did not orbit the Moon, but its flyby went farther out than the Apollo missions had.

paragraphs.heading: Missions ahead
paragraphs.text: Artemis III, planned for late 2027, will stay in Earth orbit, where its crew will practice docking with one or both of the commercial landers, Starship HLS from SpaceX and Blue Moon from Blue Origin, and test Axiom's AxEMU spacesuit. Artemis IV, planned for early 2028, is meant to be the first American crewed Moon landing since Apollo 17 in December 1972. A support flight will first place a lander in lunar orbit; the astronauts will then ride it down, make at least two spacewalks on the surface, and go back up to meet Orion for the trip home. Artemis V, in late 2028, is planned as the second landing and the point when NASA expects to start building its Moon base.

paragraphs.heading: The bigger goal
paragraphs.text: From Artemis V on, NASA intends to land on the Moon about once a year to build up a permanent base, as a step toward sending people to Mars. Planners have even thought about sending an archive of cultural works from creators around the world, called the Lunar Codex, to the Moon. Some choices, such as using a near-rectilinear halo orbit and the plans for long-term sustainability, have drawn criticism.
